He who undertakes the vow of studentship (*brahmacarya*) indeed enters upon a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*).

The fuel-stick (*samidh*) he places when entering [the vow] is the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīyā*); that which he places when about to bathe is the concluding offering (*udayanīyā*); and those which he places in between are his sacrificial sessions (*sattra*).

When a Brāhmaṇa, entering upon the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), enters the beings in four parts: one part into the fire, one part into death, one part into the teacher, and his fourth part remains in himself. When he places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire, he thereby ransoms that very part of himself which is in the fire; having consecrated it, he takes it into himself, and it enters him.

Now, when he makes himself poor, becomes shameless, begs for alms, and practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he thereby ransoms that foot of his which is in Death; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.
Then, when he obeys the word of the teacher (*ācārya*), he thereby ransoms that foot of his which is in the teacher; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.

Now, as for the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*): whatever portion of it exists within his own self, that very thing he purchases by means of it; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters into him.
(BaudhŚS 1.2.4.7–6) Indeed, one who has performed the ritual bath (*snāta*) should not beg.

by being ascetic and vigilant, one is then liberated from that sin.

"For it is known that on the days of the lunar changes (*parvan*), Rākṣasas and Piśācas become prone to transgression."
On account of other extraordinary portents and calamities as well, there shall be no study for a day and a night, except when one's mind is otherwise engaged.
Baudhāyana 1.11.21: Even in the case of mental [conception], there is a suspension of Vedic study upon birth and death.
Now, they also cite this:
"The eighth day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the fifteenth day destroys knowledge. Therefore, one should avoid [studying] on these festival days (*parvan*)."
Therefore, one should avoid [sexual intercourse] on the day of the full moon or new moon.
Now, therefore, follow the expiations.
A killer of an embryo [must perform penance] for twelve years.

Carrying a skull and a staff, wearing a donkey skin, and making his dwelling in the forest, he should set up a banner consisting of a human head at a cremation ground and have a hut constructed there;
he should live in that hut.
Wandering for alms among seven houses while proclaiming his own deed, he should sustain his life by that means alone.
Having failed to obtain the fast.
He should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Gosava, or the Agniṣṭut.
Or he may purify himself at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Now, they also cite this:
"By killing a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally, one becomes defiled according to dharma;
the seers prescribe an expiation for that act when it was not preceded by deliberate intent."
For one who kills intentionally, no atonement is found.
"Having struck [another], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; in the case of causing a fall, the *atikṛcchra*;
and in the case of blood flowing, both the *kṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Therefore, one should never strike another, nor should one cause blood to flow."
For a Kṣatriya, it is nine years.
A Vaiśya has three.
For a Śūdra, [the period of impurity lasts] one year.
And [the same applies] for a woman.
The ritual for the Ātreyī woman is to be performed as prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa woman.
One who has violated the teacher's bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed.
Or he should embrace a glowing iron image.
Alternatively, having cut off the male organ together with the testicles and holding it in his joined palms, he should walk between the southern and western directions until he collapses.
A thief, having disheveled his hair and taken a mallet made of *sīdhraka* wood, should go to the king with it upon his shoulder, saying, "Slay me with this.
With that [mallet], the king should strike him.
Now they also cite this:
"Taking a club upon his shoulder, a thief should follow the king, saying:
'O King, remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya, punish me with this.'"
"Whether in punishment or in release, the thief is freed from his guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of that thief. Thus [it is said].
Having drunk *surā*, one should burn the body with hot [liquor].
If one drinks [Soma] unintentionally, one should perform a quarter of the Kṛcchra penance for a year and undergo re-initiation.
And there is no lapse regarding the shaving, the vows, or the restrictive observances, because they have already been performed previously.
Now they also cite [this]:
"Having unintentionally drunk [the wine] of Varuṇa, or having consumed urine or feces,
a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya deserves to undergo the rite of re-consecration."
If one drinks water that has stood overnight in a vessel used for keeping *surā* liquor,
he should subsist for six days on milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
If one who has been commissioned by his teacher should die, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
This same [procedure applies] when it has not been consecrated.
For a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), the suspension of his vows (*vratāvṛtti*) occurs upon performing the funeral rites for anyone other than his mother, father, or teacher.
If he should fall ill, he may, at his will, consume all the remains of his teacher's food for the purpose of medicine.
With whatever [means] he may desire, by that he should treat [the patient].
When he is ill, having risen, he should worship the sun with this [verse]: "The swan dwelling in purity... and so forth.
Having emitted semen during the day, one should drink water that reaches the heart three times with the *retasyā* verses.
A student of sacred knowledge who approaches a woman is an *avakīrṇin*.
He should immolate a donkey as the sacrificial animal.
The animal victim and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) are dedicated to Nirṛti; their presiding deity is either Rakṣas or Yama.
"It is known from the Śiśna that they proceed with the *prāśitra* and the portions [of the victim] in the waters" (BaudhŚS 2.1.1.33).
Alternatively, on the night of the new moon, having kindled the fire and performed the ritual procedures for a wood-oblation (*dārvihoma*), he offers two oblations of clarified butter:
"O Kāma, I have transgressed; I have transgressed, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā!"
"I am oppressed by desire, I am oppressed! O Desire, to Desire, svāhā! Thus [he says].
Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence, he should address the fire from a slightly oblique position:
"May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me."
May this fire sprinkle him with long life and with strength; may it make him long-lived.
Then, while he is in the assembly, his kinsmen should pour out a vessel of water, saying, "I, being such-and-such, [am now purified].
After he has performed the ritual, having begun with water, milk, ghee, honey, and salt, the Brahmins should say to him, "It has been performed by you."
"Yes," the other replied;
"they should perform the *savanīya* sacrifice as one whose transgression has been expiated."
If he should unknowingly approach a woman of the same gotra,
he should maintain her like a mother.
If she has given birth, having performed a quarter of a Kṛcchra penance for one year [reciting]:
"Whatever flaw has arisen in my self... [she becomes pure].
Furthermore, one should offer oblations with these two [verses]: "Agni has given back the eye."
The younger brother who marries before his elder, the elder brother who is thus superseded,
and the woman who marries him— all of these go to hell, with the giver and the officiating priest as the fifth.

The one who has been superseded by a younger brother, the one who supersedes, the giver [of the girl], and he who performs the sacrifice for them—all these are purified by a twelve-night Kṛcchra penance; a woman is purified by a three-night penance. Thus it is said.
Now, the acts leading to loss of caste (patanīya).
Baudhāyana 2.1.2.2: A voyage upon the ocean.
Theft of a Brahmin’s property or the misappropriation of a trust.
Falsehood regarding land.
Dealing in all kinds of merchandise.
Serving Śūdras.
Baudhāyana 2.1.2.7: Offspring born of a Śūdra woman.
And there is also the state of being his offspring.
Having performed one of these [rites].
Eating measured portions at the fourth meal-time, they should descend into the water according to the ritual procedure for the Soma-pressings;
by alternating between standing and sitting, they destroy that evil within three years.

Whatever sin a Brāhmaṇa incurs by associating with one of dark complexion for a single night, he destroys that sin in three years by eating only at the fourth meal-time and subsisting on water. Thus it is said.
Now, the minor offenses (upapātaka).

Baudhāyana 2.1.2.13: Having had sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, one who has lost her caste, or an outcast; practicing medicine, officiating at sacrifices for a village, subsisting by the stage, being a teacher of acting, tending cattle and buffaloes, and whatever else is of a similar nature, as well as defiling a maiden—[these constitute secondary sins].
Their means of subsistence, however, shall be the conduct of an outcast for two years.
Now, the things that cause impurity.

Gambling, sorcery, living by gleaning for one who has not established the sacred fires, the practice of begging for one who has returned home from his teacher’s house, his continued residence in the teacher’s house beyond four months, teaching him [the Vedas], and the pointing out of the lunar mansions.
Baudh2.1.2.17: Their atonement, however, consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days,
twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, six days, three days, one day and night, and one day— according to the repetition of the ritual acts.

Now, those who have fallen [from their caste], having come together, should practice the duties [of outcasts]: acting as priests for one another, teaching one another, and intermarrying among themselves.
Having produced sons, they should say: "Depart from us; in this way you shall attain the status of Aryas."
Moreover, one does not fall [from caste] as long as one's sense organs remain intact.
This is to be understood by means of this:
even one who is deficient in a limb may produce a child with all limbs complete.
"Because it gives birth."
Hārīta says that this is false.
Women should share the same status as a vessel for curd.
For if one churns impure milk that has been curdled in such a vessel, the learned do not employ it for religious rites.
In this way, when impure semen is emitted, there is no sexual union with it.
For those born from impure semen, if they so desire, there is an expiation.
For those who have committed acts leading to loss of caste, the third part [of the penance] applies to women; their share is one-third.
Now they also cite this:
"Whatever one does with sesame seeds other than eating them, anointing oneself, or giving them away,
one becomes a worm in dog dung."
Having become a worm, he sinks down together with his ancestors. Thus it is said.
He who sells sesame seeds sells his ancestors;
he who sells rice grains sells his vital breaths;
and he who, for the sake of profit, gives away his daughter in marriage sells his portions of merit.
Grass and wood that are unaltered may be sold.
Now they also cite this:
"Animals with only one row of teeth, stone extracted from salt,
this, O Brāhmaṇa, is your merchandise, as well as thread not yet spun into cloth."

Or, excluding those for mortal sins (*pātaka*), one should pour clarified butter over a tawny, reddish-brown cow with long hair, scatter black sesame seeds over it, and give her to a learned Brahmin (*anūcāna*).
Or, he may perform the rite for twelve days with the Kūṣmāṇḍa formulas.
"By this, he is released from whatever sin prior to the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*)."
If one is falsely accused of a mortal sin (pātaka), the penance is a Kṛcchra.
That year belongs to the one who pronounces the curse.
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for one year through officiating at sacrifices,
teaching, or marriage, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
The penance for consuming impure substances is the *naiṣpurīṣya* rite;
that is accomplished within seven nights.
Water, milk, ghee, and air—consuming these hot substances for three days each constitutes the *sataptakṛcchra* penance.
Eating only in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening for three days,
eating only what is unasked for for another three days, and fasting for the final three days— this is the Parāka Kṛcchra penance.
Eating only what is unasked for in the morning and evening constitutes the *parāka* penance; these three types of four-night penances constitute the *kṛcchra* for women, children, and the elderly.
One should eat as much as one can take in a single mouthful; this is the *atikṛcchra* penance, as described previously.
The third [type] consists of subsisting on water; that is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
In the Kṛcchra penance, there is the ritual touching of water at the three sessions of the day.
Sleeping on the ground.
Wearing a single garment, and the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails.
This same [rite] applies to a woman, with the exception of shaving the hair;
with the exception of shaving the hair.

One who constantly uses water for purification, always wears the sacred thread, is constant in private Vedic study, avoids the food of a *vṛṣala*, approaches his wife only during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules— such a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman.
"The Śruti says: 'Manu divided his inheritance among his sons.'"
It is in equal portions for all, because there is no distinction made.
Or the eldest may set aside a choice portion or a choice form [of the property].
"Therefore, they exclude the eldest son from his share of the wealth"—so says the Śruti.
Or, from among ten [shares], the eldest shall set aside one for himself.
The others shall divide [the remainder] equally.
The division of the inheritance takes place with the father's consent while the father is still living.
Among the four castes, cows, horses, goats, and sheep constitute the senior share.
In the case of a coexistence of sons born of women of different castes, one should divide the inheritance into ten parts and distribute them in order as four, three, two, and one.
But when a legitimate son of the body (aurasa) has been born, those of the same caste (savarṇāḥ) shall take a third share.
Between the son of a wife of equal caste and the son of a wife of the next lower caste, if the son of the next lower caste is virtuous, he shall take the share of the eldest.
For one who possesses excellence is indeed the sustainer of the others.
One should know the son begotten by oneself upon a wife of the same caste who has been consecrated as the *aurasa* (legitimate) son.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"From limb after limb you are born; from the heart you arise."
"Thou art indeed my very self, O son; live for a hundred autumns! [Thus he says.
Regarding a daughter born of a *putrikā* marriage, one should understand that the son born of her is a *putrikā-putra*, while any other son born of her is a *dauhitra*.

Now they also cite [this]: "The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-suta) should designate his mother at the first rice-ball offering, her father at the second, and her grandfather at the third. Thus it is said.
He who is begotten on the wife of one who is dead, impotent, or diseased, with the consent of another, is a *kṣetraja* (son of the soil).
This man, having two fathers and two gotras, becomes an heir to the *svadhā* offerings and the inheritance of both.
Now they also cite:
"In the case of one who has two fathers, there should be the offering of rice balls for both; on each rice ball, the names of both should be mentioned.
Thus, three rice balls shall be offered for six [ancestors]; by acting in this way, one does not go astray."
One who is given by both his mother and father, or by either one of them, and is accepted for the sake of offspring, is a *datta* (given) son.
One whom he himself, out of desire, makes his own similar [son] is the *kṛtrima* (adopted son).
One born secretly in the house and discovered at the end is a *gūḍhaja* (secret-born son).
One who, having been abandoned by both his mother and father, or by either one of them, is taken up for the sake of offspring, is an *apaviddha*.
If one should approach a woman who has not been consecrated for marriage and has not been given away in marriage, the son born of her is a *kānīna*.
If a woman who is pregnant is consecrated—whether her condition is known or unknown—the son born of her is a *sahoḍha*.
One who is purchased from the hands of his mother and father, or from either one of them, and is taken for the sake of offspring, is a "bought" (krīta) son.
If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcaste husband, finds another husband, the son born of her as a *paunarbhavī* is called a *paunarbhava*.
One who, being deprived of mother and father, gives himself away of his own accord is a *svayamdatta* (self-given son).
One born from a Śūdra woman by a man of the twice-born castes who belongs to the same *pravara* lineage as the father is a Niṣāda.
The *pāraśava* is [born] from desire; these are the sons.

Now they also cite [the following]: "The son of the body (*aurasa*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the son given (*datta*), the son made (*kṛtrima*),
the son born in secret (*gūḍhaja*), and the son cast off (*apaviddha*)— these they declare to be the sharers of the inheritance."

The son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son received with a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), the purchased son (*krīta*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the self-given son (*svayaṃdatta*), and the *niṣāda*— these they declare to be sharers of the lineage (*gotrabhāj*).
"Aupajaṅghani says that among those [options], it should be the very first one."
"O Janaka, I do not envy women now as I did before,
since they have declared in the abode of Yama that a son belongs to the progenitor."
"The seed-bearer leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, one should protect one's own wife."
Fearing the seed of others, they guard themselves.
"Be vigilant; guard this thread! Let not others' seeds be sown in your field.
In the hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor."
One who knows this [truth] regarding saṃsāra makes this thread futile. Thus it is said.
Until they reach the age of legal majority, their shares, along with the interest thereon, shall be kept strictly guarded by them.
They shall support those whose legal affairs have passed away with food and clothing.
And also those who are blind, mentally dull, eunuchs, addicted to vices, diseased, and so forth.
Those who do not perform the ritual acts.
With the exception of those who have fallen from their caste and those born of them.
There is no social interaction with those who have fallen from their caste.
But even if his mother has fallen [from her caste], he should support her without speaking to her.
The daughters shall receive their mother's ornaments, whether they were part of the traditional inheritance or otherwise.
A woman possesses no independence.
Now they also cite:
"The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth; but the son protects her in old age."
In old age, a woman does not deserve independence. Thus it is said.
"For women are considered to be devoid of sensory power and without inheritance," so says the Śruti.
Striving for the welfare of their husband, they shall win the heavenly world.
In the event of a transgression, the penance is a *kṛcchra*.
And for a Śūdra, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the case of those born in the reverse order from Vaiśyas and others, one should perform the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and other such penances.
For males, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) shall last for one year.
One should burn a Śūdra with a fire from a mat (or a fire from a funeral pyre).
Now, moreover, they cite [the following]:
For a non-Brāhmaṇa, corporal punishment shall be the penalty for adultery.
For all social classes alike, one's wife is more worthy of protection than one's wealth.
But there is no execution for those who are the wives of performers, nor for those on the stage;
for they cause these men to mingle and even lead them away while they are well-concealed.
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menses carry away their sins.
Soma gave them purity;
Gandharva gave them eloquent speech;
and Agni gave them the power to consume all things.
Therefore, women are free from all blemish and may eat all things that are edible.

One should abandon a wife who bears no offspring in the tenth year, one whose offspring are all female in the twelfth year, one whose offspring die in the fifteenth year, but one who speaks unpleasantly immediately.
For one year, the widow of the deceased shall avoid honey, meat, liquor, and salt, and she shall sleep on the ground.
"For six months," says Maudgalya.
From this point forward, with the permission of her elders, a woman without a son may procreate a son through her husband's brother.
Now they also cite this [verse]: "A barren cow,
one that has already given birth, one that is without menses, and one whose offspring has passed away— one who is unwilling should not be employed [as a victim], for no fruit is found in her."

A maternal uncle’s sister, a paternal aunt, a sister, a sister’s daughter, a daughter-in-law, a maternal aunt, and a female friend’s wife—these are women who must not be approached for sexual intercourse.
For approaching women who should not be approached, the expiation consists of the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
By this, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained.
Now they also cite this:

"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Caṇḍālī woman, or having eaten [with her], or having accepted a gift [from her], falls from his status through ignorance; but through knowledge, he would attain equality [with her]."
"By approaching through negligence the wife of one's father, teacher, or king, one becomes a violator of the Guru's bed; the atonement for this has been previously stated. Thus it is said.
If he is unable to subsist by teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts, he may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, because that is the next in order.
"No," says Gautama;
for the duty of a Kṣatriya is exceedingly fierce for a Brāhmaṇa.
Now they also cite this example:
"For the sake of cows, for the sake of Brahmins, or even upon the confusion of castes,
a Brahmin and a Vaiśya may take up arms out of regard for righteousness."
The livelihood of a Vaiśya should be practiced [by him], because it is the one immediately preceding [his own].
Before the morning meal, he should be a ploughman.

[He should perform the rite] with two goats whose nostrils have not been pierced and which possess testicles, without piercing them with a needle and repeatedly encouraging them by shouting. The fire begins with the wife;
the performance of the ritual acts in that fire takes place prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).

Baudhāyana 2.2.4.23: From the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) onwards, these [rites] are perpetual (*ajasra*): namely, the *agnyādheya*, the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the animal sacrifice at the solstices (*udagayana* and *dakṣiṇāyana*), the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* offering at the beginning of the seasons, and the *jyotiṣṭoma* in the spring; in this manner, one attains security (*kṣema*).
Now they also cite this:
"Neither by one habituated to sleeping during the day, nor by one who eats all kinds of food,
nor by one who has fallen from a high station, can it be possible to go to heaven at will."
One should avoid wretchedness, deceit, and crookedness.
Now, moreover, in this regard they cite the verse from the dialogue between Uśanas and Vṛṣaparvan’s two daughters:
“You are indeed the daughter of one who praises, who begs, and who accepts;
whereas I am the son of one who is praised, who gives, and who does not accept.”
"Of one who gives but does not accept," so [it is said].
The ascetic practice consists of immersion in water.
Having gratified the deities, he performs the libation for the ancestors.
He pours out water along the bank with the verse,
"Carrying strength."
Now, they also cite this:
"When the flowing rivers are unobstructed, the three twice-born castes,
having risen in the morning..."
Having risen in the morning, they should perform the libations for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
When the waters are obstructed, they shall not perform [the rite]; in that case, the builder of the embankment has no share.
Therefore, one should avoid bridges and wells constructed by others.
Now, they also cite [the following]:
"Or, having drawn out three lumps [of earth], one should perform [the rite] in times of distress, but not always;
however, when [water] is obstructed, one should likewise take three lumps of clay from a well and three jars of water."

Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having accepted much that should be accepted; or having officiated at a sacrifice for one for whom one should not officiate; or having eaten the food of one whose food should not be eaten—one should recite the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
Now they also cite this:
"Those who mix with their teachers and those who mix with their pupils,
who are confused in their food and mantras, enter into long-lasting darkness."
Now follow the observances of the Snātaka.

In the evening and in the morning, having offered the Vaiśvadeva oblation with whatever food is fit for consumption, he should honor Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have arrived as guests according to his ability;
if he is unable to do so for many, he should give to one who possesses good qualities.
Or rather, it should be whichever one arrived first.
If a Śūdra has arrived, one should employ him in the work.
Or he should give the first portion to one learned in the Vedas.
A distribution of shares is ordained for those who are permanent dependents, provided it does not cause hardship to them.
But one must never, under any circumstances, eat without having first given [to others].
Now, moreover, they cite two verses regarding food in this regard:
"He who, without having given to me— to the ancestors, the deities, his servants, guests, and his circle of friends— "
Eating what is prepared as if it were poison out of delusion—him I devour; Death am I for him.
Having offered the Agnihotra and performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he who— having honored his guests and provided for his dependents—
eats what remains with contentment, purity, and faith, for him I become nectar, and he enjoys me.

Baudhāyana 2.3.5.19: A distribution of property according to one's ability should be made to those who are not merely nominal Brahmins but are learned (*śrotriya*) and have mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*), as well as to those seeking funds for their teacher, those needing medicine, those whose livelihood is exhausted, those intending to perform a sacrifice, those engaged in Vedic study, those traveling on a journey, and those participating in the Vaiśvajita rite—provided they are begging outside the sacrificial altar.
In the case of the others, [the offering] consists of prepared food.

Having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, having sipped water for purification, and having taken up the food brought to him in a clean, enclosed place, he should eat it— having cast away desire, anger, malice, greed, and delusion— using all his fingers and making no sound.
One should not discard the remainder of the rice balls into the vessel.
If one consumes food mixed with meat, fish, or sesame seeds, one should touch water and then touch fire.
And after sunset, there is a bath.
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*.
One should not eat food from the lap.
One should not eat while seated on a chair.
He should carry a staff made of bamboo, as well as a golden ornament and earrings.
One should avoid washing one's feet with the foot itself and stepping upon it.
One should not wear a garland outside [the garment].
One should not look at the sun at either sunrise or sunset.
One should not point out a rainbow to another, saying, "It is Indra's bow."
If he should say, "The jewel-bow," he should simply say, "The jewel-bow."
One should not pass between the Indra-kīla pillar and the crossbar at the city gate.
One should not pass between the two *pleṅkha* swings.
And one should not walk over the cord for the calf.
One should not step upon ashes, bones, hair, chaff, potsherds, or the water used for ritual bathing.
One should not tell another person that a cow is suckling her calf.
One should not say of a non-cow, "She is a cow."
If he should say, "A cow that is to be," he should simply say, "A cow that is to be."
One should not speak words that are bitter, harsh, or rough.
One should not travel along a road alone.
Not with outcasts, nor with a woman, nor with a Śūdra.
One should not go out at evening.
One should not bathe naked.
One should not bathe at night.
One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
One should not look into a well.
One should not look into a pit.
He should not sit down there where someone else might make him rise.
A path must be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, to a cow, to a king, to one who is sightless,
to an elderly person, to one oppressed by a heavy burden, to a pregnant woman, and to one who is weak.

A righteous person should strive to settle in a village that has abundant fuel, water, barley, fodder, firewood, and *kuśa* grass; where garlands are available; which is accessible for going out; which is crowded with wealthy people; which is prosperous through industry; which is predominantly inhabited by noble persons; and which is inaccessible to bandits.
In a village where the water comes from a well, a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman,
having lived there for twelve years, attains the same status as a Śūdra.
With his body covered in the dust of the city, his eyes and face completely filled with it, and dwelling in the city with a well-restrained self— he will attain perfection; that is not so.
The dust of chariots, horses, elephants, grain, and cows is auspicious;

Whatever sin has been committed by the generative organ, or whatever has been done by the feet,
by the arms, by the mind, by speech, or by the ear, skin, nose, and eyes— [all that is purified].
Alternatively, in the event of transgressions involving the eye, ear, skin, nose, or mind, one is purified by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

In the case of eating the food of a Śūdra, sexual intercourse with a woman [of forbidden class], or eating [forbidden food] alone—each of these separately—one should perform seven breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for seven days each.

In the case of consuming what is not to be eaten, not to be consumed, not to be drunk, or not to be swallowed; likewise, in the sale of goods that should not be sold—with the exception of honey, meat, clarified butter, oil, alkali, salt, and inferior food—and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for each of those acts over a period of twelve days.

In cases other than mortal sins (*pātaka*), sins causing loss of caste (*patanīya*), and minor offenses (*upapātaka*), as well as any other similar acts, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for each half-month.

One should give a maiden who is still pre-pubertal (*nagnikā*) to a virtuous man who observes celibacy;
or else, one may give her even to one lacking in virtues, but one must not allow her to remain until she has reached her menses.
He who does not give away a maiden who has reached puberty within three years undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo.
"If he does not beg [for alms], it is thus; but if he begs, Manu has declared that there is a fault—a mortal sin—for each and every season."
A woman who has reached puberty should wait for her father’s command for three years;
then, in the fourth year, she should find a suitable husband. If no suitable man is available, she may resort to one who is deficient in qualities.

If a maiden has been carried off by force, provided she has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras, she may be given to another according to the prescribed rule; for such a girl remains exactly as a maiden.

provided she is still a virgin who has returned from her husband's house—

He who does not approach his wife when she is in her season for three years undoubtedly incurs a fault equal to that of killing an embryo.
But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him—
his ancestors lie within that menstrual flow for that entire month.
"He who does not approach his wife during her season, and he who approaches her outside the season— they both incur an equal fault, as does he who discharges semen into a place that is not the womb."
If a wife, by refusing to go to her husband’s residence, causes the loss of her fertile season,

If a man does not approach his wife— who has bathed after her menses, who is self-restrained, and who practices dharma—

Seated with purificatory grass in hand, one should practice the daily *brahman*— namely, breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), purifiers (*pavitra*), the *vyāhṛtis*, and likewise the *praṇava*.
Always disciplined, one should repeatedly perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) again and again;

Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence and standing slightly sideways before the fire, he should worship it, saying:

For three days at a time, one should drink hot milk, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass;

Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,

Restraining his self, one should perform the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* penance by eating eight morsels of sacrificial food at midday for each month.
If a twice-born man eats no more than two hundred and ninety-eight mouthfuls of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever over the course of a month, he attains the same world as the Moon.

Eating grains, oil-cakes, and buttermilk, or subsisting on barley-water and water, and fasting by eating only air—
